turns.zh: 这是一个非常重要的观点，也是一种很好的思考方式。这让我想起了安迪·约翰斯（Andy Johns）在节目中提到的例子，说明生活中许多看似微不足道的小事，最终会堆积成难以承受的压力，导致他无法维持现有的生活方式。（00:36:34）：本期节目由Miro赞助。您是否曾觉得自己的项目组织得不够理想，或者团队成员很难找到所需的文档、文件和项目背景信息？Miro能助您优化工作流程、整理信息，并让整个团队保持同步。如果您想了解Miro能为您带来哪些帮助，不妨看看我与Miro团队共同创建的Miro看板，其中包含我最喜欢的即插即用模板，如用户旅程地图、最喜欢的单页提案模板，以及头脑风暴指南。我的看板还为您提供了分享播客建议的空间，并为我提出的问题答疑。您可以轻松创建自己的Miro看板，感受其便捷性。别忘了体验一些实用功能，如便签、内嵌评论和图表，以及超酷的图表绘制工具。请访问miro.com/lenny。今日注册，即可免费使用前三块Miro看板。让Miro为您最复杂的项目注入简洁力量。访问m-i-r-o.com/lenny。（00:37:40）：您能举些这种微小信号的例子吗？所以您的建议是，留意这些表明自己当前生活不可持续的细微迹象。比如，可能需要做出改变的信号有哪些？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah, so I'll tie this in with a concept that I call emotional debt, which is basically when our nervous system experiences stress, there's known as a mobilization cycle, and if that cycle isn't completed or we don't get to downshift or relax on the other side, that gets stored in the body as allostatic load, which I call emotional debt. And over time, that creates fragility in the nervous system. And so what that fragility can look like is anything from being impacted by small things in a kind of disproportionate way. So noticing that you are more reactive than normal, maybe you're a little bit more snappy, maybe you get frustrated by little things, maybe your sleep isn't as good, maybe you wake up not feeling fully rested. Maybe relationships are often, especially intimate relationships are usually a place that this shows up or relationships at work. So those are the classic early warning signs. And then as that emotional debt threshold increases in the same way that say with technical debt, if you're building a product in the beginning, it's fine, and in fact it's even necessary in the beginning. It's great that our body can buffer the stress response because it allows us to function. But if we don't pay off that technical debt or emotional debt, then over time it accumulates and it can also come out through health crises, health challenges. It just gets basically progressively worse until that debt is paid off.
turns.zh: 是的，我要把这与我所说的情绪债务概念联系起来。基本上，当我们的神经系统经历压力时，会进入一种被称为动员周期的状态。如果这个周期未能完成，或者我们未能在另一端放松下来，情绪债务就会以非应激性负荷的形式储存在体内。久而久之，这会削弱神经系统的韧性。这种脆弱性可能表现为对微小事物反应过度、情绪易激动、因小事而烦躁、睡眠质量差、醒来时未能充分休息等症状。这种情况常出现在亲密关系中，尤其是职场关系中。所以这些都是典型的早期预警信号。随着情绪债务门槛的提高，就如同技术债务一样。如果你在项目初期积累技术债务，短期内问题不大，但如果不及时清偿债务，随着时间推移，债务会不断累积，最终可能通过健康危机、健康问题爆发而显现，直到债务被彻底清偿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like a lot of people listening are like, "Yes, I know exactly what you mean." How does one notice that you're building emotional debt and then how do you start to release this debt and pay off this debt?
turns.zh: 我感觉很多听众会说：“是的，我完全明白你的意思。” 那如何察觉自己正在积累情绪债务，又该如何开始释放和偿还这些债务呢？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: What I've seen with some of my founder clients and in the research that we did where we interviewed 260 leaders, what can often happen is that emotional debt will increase and increase and increase until it gets to a point where we are well outside what's known as a window of tolerance. And at that point there's like a crash. It's almost like the fuse switch blows and there's exhaustion. Maybe there's complete inability to get up off the couch. And for some people, people with large nervous system capacity, they can keep going for five years, maybe 10 years, and they can keep building this up, and it becomes normalized to live in a way where you are always on and never really relaxing or coming down. Or one really key sign actually is if you are not able to naturally downshift or down regulate your nervous system at the end of the day without something like wine or CBD or some kind of external substance, that's a sign that you kind of reached a certain threshold of emotional debt.
turns.zh: 就我对一些创业者客户的观察，以及我们在研究中对260位领导者进行访谈的结果来看，情感债务往往会不断累积，直到超出所谓的“容忍区间”。此时，人往往会崩溃，就像保险丝烧断，精疲力竭，严重者甚至无法从沙发上起身。有些神经系统能力强大的人或许能坚持五年、十年，不断积累压力，直至将这种状态常态化——时刻保持紧绷状态，从不真正放松或休整。还有一个关键信号：如果你无法在一天结束时自然地让神经系统降温或调节到正常状态，非得借助酒精、CBD或其他外部物质才能做到，那就意味着你的情感债务已经达到了某个临界值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then how does one start to pay off this debt if you've spent years just working way too hard, you've had a relationship that just isn't working great, I don't know. I imagine most people go to therapy and just talk through all these things and try to work through the challenges. What do you recommend if you're just like, "Man, I feel like I have this, what should I do?"
turns.zh: 那么，如果你多年来一直过度劳累，或者陷入一段不尽如人意的感情关系，该如何开始偿还这笔债务呢？我猜大多数人会选择心理治疗，倾诉心事、克服挑战。但如果你只想说：“天啊，我感觉自己深陷其中，我该怎么办？”该如何应对呢？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah, well, I mean that's a big question. I'll probably get some pushback for this, but I'm not a big fan of talk therapy alone or at least therapy that doesn't have a somatic or body-based component. And from my understanding of the nervous system and how we store this stress, just talking about things and keeping things on the level of the intellect doesn't actually address the root of the challenge. What we need to do is create a certain sense of safety to kind of go into those buffered emotional responses and feel them all the way through and allow that mobilization reflex to complete. (00:41:48): And so to kind of give a personal example, when I was living in Bali, I did several hundred breathwork journeys where you breathe in a certain way to get into an altered state, and then in that place, these memories would arise of these things that happened 5, 10 years ago. And my body, it would either move a certain way or the anger would come through. Sometimes there would be sadness or grief. Often there's a lot of stored emotion that's held in our body that just needs permission to kind of be felt through and be released. And so for me, it was a journey of coming into right relationship with my anger and my grief, and honestly my shame as well, giving myself permission to feel this gunk that had been stored in my pelvis. (00:42:35): So I'm not saying you have to go to Bali and do 200 breathwork journeys. That's definitely not... I mean, that's a path. But first it begins with, as I said, cultivating interoception and even being aware that there is this tension, there are these things in your body. Secondly, having the practices of self-regulation so that if these things come up, you don't get overwhelmed. You're able to downshift and ground. And then thirdly, it's the practice of what I call emotional fluidity, which is basically creating the conditions of welcoming the full spectrum of emotions as they arise. And often it's very helpful to have a guide or a somatic practitioner, I like somatic experiencing, hakomi, the two modalities I'm a big fan of. And yeah, that's the journey and a process and it depends how many years you've been operating in a slightly numbed way, and it's different for everyone. But it begins by tuning into and listening to the body and then having honestly curiosity about what is there and just following that curiosity and the body starts to show you what is ready to be seen.
turns.zh: 是啊，好吧，我觉得这是一个很重要的问题。我这么说可能会招来反对，但我不太喜欢单纯的谈话疗法，或者至少是不带有躯体或基于身体疗法的疗法。根据我对神经系统的理解，以及我们储存压力的方式，光是谈论问题、让事情停留在理智层面，并不能真正解决问题的根源。我们需要创造一种安全感，让人们能深入那些被压抑的情绪反应，彻底感受它们，并让动员反射得以完成。（00:41:48）举个个人例子吧，我在巴厘岛生活时，进行了数百次呼吸训练——通过特定方式呼吸以进入一种改变的状态。在那种状态下，我会回忆起5、10年前发生的事情。我的身体要么会做出某种反应，要么愤怒情绪会涌现。有时会有悲伤或悲恸。通常，我们体内积压着大量情绪，需要得到许可才能彻底释放它们。对我来说，这是一次与愤怒、悲恸，甚至羞耻建立正确关系的旅程，让自己允许那些积压在骨盆中的负面情绪得以释放。（00:42:35）我不是说你必须去巴厘岛做200次呼吸训练。这当然不是必需的……但首先要从培养内感知开始，甚至要意识到身体里存在着紧张感和未被处理的情绪。其次，要掌握自我调节的技巧，这样当这些情绪涌现时，你就不会感到不知所措。能够调整状态、接地气。第三，就是我所说的情绪流动性练习，简单来说就是创造条件，欢迎所有涌现的情绪。通常，有一位导师或躯体疗法从业者会很有帮助，比如躯体体验疗法、哈科米疗法——这两种疗法我都很推崇。是的，这是一段旅程，也是一个过程。它取决于你以某种麻木状态生活了多少年，而且每个人的情况不同。但它始于倾听身体的声音，诚实地好奇身体里有什么，然后顺着这种好奇心，身体会告诉你哪些情绪已经准备好被看见了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that it always comes back to the original place we started which is that the way we feel is a very bottom up body-based system, it's not we feel something and our body gets nervous. It's our body gets nervous, and they're like, "Oh, here's why I'm nervous." And your advice is just focus a lot on helping your body release the stuff that you've built up this debt. And then also just when you're nervous in the moment, focus on getting your body to a state versus trying to convince your mind now everything's going to be okay.
turns.zh: 我喜欢你最后总能回归到最初的观点——我们的感受是一个自下而上的基于身体的系统，不是我们感觉到某种情绪然后身体才紧张。实际上是身体先紧张起来，然后身体会说：“哦，这就是我紧张的原因。” 你的建议就是要专注于帮助身体释放积压的情绪负担。还有，当你当下感到紧张时，要专注于让身体进入一种平静状态，而不是试图说服自己一切都会好起来。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And specifically on the therapy route, just to touch on that, so your advice there is if you were to work with a therapist and you feel a lot of this stuff that we're talking about is focused on a somatic oriented therapy where it's body oriented, not just thinking about it and talking through stuff, it's actually convincing your body, "Here's a way to helping your body release this debt, essentially."
turns.zh: 具体说到治疗路径，你的建议是，如果你找治疗师治疗，感觉到很多我们讨论的这些情绪问题，都要选择基于躯体导向的疗法——而不仅仅是思考和谈论问题，而是真正让身体相信：“这里有一种帮助你释放情绪债务的方法。”

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, you can understand in precise detail about whatever the challenge was from 5, 10 and 15 years ago, but if you're unable to connect it to the correlating sensations in the body... Usually if say, I don't know, if I was to imagine someone shouted at me yesterday and I think about that, there's usually a correlating kind of sematic sensation. The neuroscientist Damasio calls it a somatic marker. So by tracking the somatic markers and then either on your own just kind of following that sensation and allowing whatever emotion was present at the time to complete that is the way that we kind of slowly pay off that emotional debt by one process at a time.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，你可以精确地回想起5、10、15年前遇到的挑战，但如果你无法将其与身体产生的相关感觉联系起来……通常来说，比如说，我不知道，如果我想象昨天有人对我大喊大叫，然后回想起来，这种情况通常会有一种对应的情绪感觉。神经科学家达马西奥称之为躯体标记。因此，通过追踪这些躯体标记，然后顺着这种感觉，允许当时存在的任何情绪得以释放，这就是我们逐步化解情绪债务的方式——一次处理一个过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So maybe coming back to this question of say someone is listening and wondering, am I building emotional debt? Am I ignoring things that are these feathers? What are signs and just, I don't know, examples of emotional debt being built up of this trauma, whatever you want to call it, being built up in the body? I don't know, is it just like anytime you feel really nervous, that's emotional debt? Is it anytime you push something down that you are pretty sure you should deal with in the moment, that's emotional debt? What are just some examples of what that feels like and looks like?
turns.zh: 那么，回到这个问题：假设有人正在听，心里想，我是否正在积累情绪债务？我是否忽视了那些细微的情绪信号？有哪些迹象和例子能说明这种创伤（无论你怎么称呼它）在身体里积聚的情绪债务？我不知道，是不是每次你感到非常紧张，那就是情绪债务？或者每次你强行压抑某个本该当下处理的事情，那也是情绪债务？这些情绪累积的感觉和表现具体是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah, so it's typically different forms of nervous system dysregulation and that shows up as it could be someone's breathing pattern if they're constantly in this sympathetic or hypervigilant state, if they're always tracking for things, looking for the worst case scenario. Another common one, and this is particularly true in the tech sector, is being very much in the head and living in the thoughts and the mind the entire time. And there's a form of disassociation that happens as a kind of protection mechanism essentially because it's uncomfortable to be with the sensations in the body. And because our society tends to reward people for solving problems and being in their mind, that is a pattern that continues for many, many years or even decades. (00:46:43): Other ones are, I think the most obvious one for people is emotional reactivity, where your response to a certain situation is disproportionate to what's happened. So for example, if you said something to me of that doesn't make any sense, and I was like, I freeze maybe... And this is another important point that most people have two versions of reactivity. Some people will freeze, withdraw, shut down and disconnect, and other people will become more aggressive, become bigger and attack and fight back. And knowing which way you tend to orient, for me, it's usually shrink and freeze and shut down, knowing what your pattern is and also knowing what the sensations are when this happens, it's really helpful for you to be like, "Oh, that thing's happening." My priority now is to downshift and kind of find a sense of safety basically in the body and then interact, then make the decision, then have the conversation. Because if you can keep going from that place of reactivity, nothing good happens from that place. No great decisions were made from that place. So again, that's a place where having the interoceptive awareness to know, "Oh, this is what's going on." Being able to then downshift your system, kind of access a sense of, "Oh, I'm okay, actually this isn't so bad." And then moving on from there is a profoundly practical and just useful skill.
turns.zh: 是的，通常表现为不同形式的神经系统失调，比如呼吸模式异常，如果一个人长期处于交感神经或高度警觉状态，总是在寻找最坏的情况；还有在科技行业很常见的过度思考，始终沉浸在思维和脑海中。还有一种解离反应，本质上是一种保护机制，因为身体的情绪感觉太令人不适了。而我们的社会往往奖励那些善于解决问题、专注思考的人，这种模式会持续多年甚至几十年。（00:46:43）其他例子包括情绪反应失调，比如对某个情境的反应与实际情况不符。例如，如果你对我说某句话，我觉得毫无道理，然后我可能直接僵住……这是一个重要点，多数人有两种反应模式。有些人会退缩、封闭、脱离；另一些人则会变得更具攻击性、变得强势并反击。了解自己的倾向模式很重要。比如我通常会退缩、封闭、脱离，知道自己的模式是什么，以及这种情绪出现时的感觉，这真的很有帮助。能意识到“哦，情绪又来了。”现在我的首要任务是调整状态，在身体里找到安全感，然后再去互动、做决定、交流。因为如果你一直处于这种反应模式中，就不会有好结果，也不会做出明智的决定。所以，拥有内感知能力，能意识到“哦，原来是这样。”然后让身体系统平静下来，意识到“其实我没事，这没那么糟糕。”从那里继续前进，这是一项非常实用且有用的技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kind of along these same lines, you wrote somewhere this idea that you have a big competitive advantage if you feel the feels is the way you described it. Does that ring a bell? And if so, what can you share around that, just why this is so powerful, especially in the workplace?
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，你在某处写道，如果你能"感同身受"（这是你描述的一种状态），就能获得巨大的竞争优势。这听起来熟悉吗？如果是这样的话，你能否谈谈为什么这如此有效，尤其是在职场中？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah, so I think I wrote about this in one of the Every essays. I think the title was The Best Decision-Making Is Emotional. And I basically wanted to kind of poke at the phrase, I think I saw someone on Twitter say, "Fact over feelings, like don't let emotions ruin good decision making." And yeah, there's so much that I can say about this. But basically there was a landmark study by this guy, Damasio, this kind of famous neuroscientist, and he studied a patient called Elliot. And Elliot had a tumor in his brain that was removed and it basically meant that he was unable to feel emotions. So his entire emotional capacity was removed. And Elliot went from being a successful married businessman to divorced, broke and unable to choose what he could have for lunch. He was unable to make the most basic life decisions, and it's because he didn't have access to that emotional sense in his brain. (00:49:22): And so our brain is like a prediction making machine, and as I mentioned earlier, there's this highway of sensory data that's coming up through the body. And if we don't listen to that when we are making decisions, then we're losing out on a lot of information. And what tends to happen, I see this in clients that I work with, is if they are avoiding feeling a certain way, let's say, that they don't enjoy feeling conflict or anger, then they will make decisions subconsciously to avoid feeling that way. And it becomes a huge bias and a huge problem because people make decisions because they're afraid of feeling a certain way. And if you are on the other hand able to just welcome and be with whatever emotions would arise on the other side of a decision, you're able to decide clearly instead of being skewed one way or the other.
turns.zh: 是啊，我记得我在《Every》系列的某篇文章中写过这个话题。标题是《最佳决策源于情感》。我当时主要想反驳那种观点——我记得在推特上有人说：“用事实而非情感做决策，别让情绪毁掉好决策。”关于这个话题我能说很多。但最关键的是达马西奥（Damasio）那项具有里程碑意义的研究。他是著名的神经科学家，研究了一位叫埃利奥特（Elliot）的患者。埃利奥特的大脑肿瘤被切除后，他完全丧失了情感能力。从成功的已婚商人变成离婚、破产、连午餐吃什么都无法决定的人。他连最基本的生活决策都无法完成，就因为大脑失去了情感感知能力。（00:49:22）所以大脑就像一个预测机器，正如我之前提到的，身体会传来大量感官数据。如果做决策时忽视这些信息，就会错失大量信息。我在客户身上看到，人们如果刻意回避某种情绪，比如不愿感受冲突或愤怒，就会下意识做出回避情绪的决策。这会形成严重的偏见和问题，因为人们因害怕某种情绪而做出错误决策。相反，如果能接纳并处理决策后的情绪波动，就能清晰判断，而非被情绪左右。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Easier said than done.
turns.zh: 说起来容易做起来难。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you find there's ever a downside to being too in touch with what you're feeling? I actually not a feeler of what I'm feeling kind of person. I'm pretty stable, partly because I'm not super in tune with what I'm feeling a lot of times, and maybe this is a huge problem that I need to deal with. But I don't know, it's worked out okay so far. I guess, do you ever find that sometimes it's okay, sometimes you don't need to know exactly every moment anything that's hurting you or causing you pain?
turns.zh: 你觉得过度感知情绪会有坏处吗？说实话，我不是个善于感知情绪的人。我情绪比较稳定，部分原因是我对自己的情绪不敏感。这或许是个需要解决的大问题。但目前看来还挺顺利的。你有没有发现，有时感知情绪没关系，有时又不需要时刻清楚伤害你的情绪来源？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah, it's a good question. And some people do have a very high interoceptive capacity, and that can be overwhelming. In which case I would recommend focusing on the breathing practices to build that capacity to downshift, so you're able to just function. And there's definitely people who are overwhelmed by the stimuli of day-to-day life being out in traffic, like they're very easily overwhelmed. And for those people working on increasing nervous system capacity to kind of hold that amount of stress, maybe it's through sauna and cold plunge, maybe it's through gentle titration of stresses and then downshifting, that's actually really valuable. (00:51:28): I'd also say that the ability to function well, this applies to a lot of high functioning people, which is probably honestly a lot of your audience. It's very helpful in the moment to, let's say something comes up, you want to be able to buffer intense emotions and say, get through the meeting, get through whatever it is. It's a very helpful skill. But if you don't, then give yourself spaciousness afterwards to downshift and allow yourself to feel whatever was brought up by that experience, you are going to be adding to this emotional debt over time. And as I mentioned, some people, it might be a year before there's some kind of breakdown, burnout. Other people, it might be longer. And usually it's more unfortunate in the longer case because it creates a long-term health crisis and then lower amount of money or time is able to repair the damage that's been done, which can be really tragic.
turns.zh: 是的，这确实是个好问题。有一些人的内感能力非常强，这可能会让人不堪重负。在这种情况下，我建议重点关注呼吸练习，以提升这种调节能力，让你能够正常运作。确实有一些人会被日常生活的各种刺激所压垮，比如在交通中就很容易感到不堪重负。对于这些人，通过增加神经系统的承受能力来应对这种压力可能是有效的，比如通过桑拿和冷水浴，或者逐步增加压力刺激并进行放松训练，这些方法都非常有价值。（00:51:28）我还要说，这种良好的功能能力适用于许多高效能人士，说实话，你们很多听众可能都属于这一类。在当下，比如当遇到突发状况时，你需要能够缓冲强烈的情绪，顺利完成会议或应对各种挑战。这是一项非常实用的技能。但如果你做不到这一点，那么之后就给自己留出充足的时间放松，处理由此产生的情绪问题，这样做久而久之会增加情绪债务。正如我所提到的，有些人可能需要一年时间才会出现崩溃或倦怠的情况，而另一些人则需要更长时间。通常，后者的情况更不幸，因为这会导致长期的健康危机，而修复所造成的损害则需要更多的时间和金钱，这实在令人悲哀。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My chat with Andy Johns is a great example of that happening.
turns.zh: 我与安迪·约翰斯的对话就是这种情况的一个很好例子。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah. And Andy's a superb example, and I love his vulnerability and honesty in what he's been through.
turns.zh: 是的。安迪就是一个绝佳的例子，我很欣赏他在经历过的事情中展现出的脆弱和诚实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think if you're interested in this topic, definitely watch that episode. Another exercise that you talk a lot about is this idea, it's called NSDR, I think. Talk about that and when that might be useful, how to go about using this tool.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为如果你对这个话题感兴趣，肯定要去看那期节目。另外，你经常提到的另一个练习叫NSDR，对吧？能讲讲这个概念吗？什么时候用它比较合适？如何运用这个工具？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah, so NSDR was a practice coined by Andrew Huberman, who you mentioned earlier. And it basically, it's a more scientific lens on the practice of yoga nidra, which is an ancient yoga practice. But I am a huge fan of it, and I do it myself most days for 15 to 20 minutes. Basically what it looks like is you lie down, put on an eye mask or a blindfold, and you listen to a guided audio. I've recorded some myself, so I can share these in the show note links.
turns.zh: 是的，NSDR是安德鲁·休伯曼（Andrew Huberman）创造的一个练习。你之前提到过他。它本质上是从更科学的角度解读古老的瑜伽练习——瑜伽休息术。但我非常喜欢它，我自己大多数日子都会做15到20分钟。基本流程是躺下，戴上眼罩或蒙眼布，听引导音频。我自己也录制了一些，可以在节目笔记链接中分享。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your voice would be so good for these, by the way. You found your calling.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，你的声音很适合做这些节目。你找到了自己的使命。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Nice, yeah. It's really fun for me to do. But basically what it involves is a guided body scan. So this is also a great way to practice interoception. It's something that I didn't mention earlier was that when there's cortisol present in our body, the cortisol basically acts as a numbing agent, so it's much harder to kind of tune into those sensations. But using this, I think it's a 14-minute guided NSDR practice, you're basically lying down, there's a guided body scan, there's relaxing music in the background. And by the end of it, you feel like you've had a two-hour nap. It feels incredible. (00:54:00): And particularly for people who myself tend to get tired in the afternoons, if you space this out, usually between 1 and 3:00 PM for me, that will give you a second wind in the afternoon and it'll mean you won't end the day collapse on the sofa. So I think it's great for improving interoception, it's good for allowing your body to downshift and relax instead of being in that kind of high tone sympathetic state all throughout the day. So it gives your body a break, and it just feels really good. Honestly, it's probably my most played practice of everything that I teach, just people listen to it every day. So I'll share that in the show notes as well.
turns.zh: 不错，确实很有趣。我特别喜欢做这个。不过这个练习主要包括引导式身体扫描。这也是练习内感知的好方法。我之前没提到的一点是，当体内有皮质醇时，它会像麻醉剂一样作用，阻碍我们感知身体的感觉。但通过这个练习，你可以完成14分钟的引导式NSDR练习，基本躺着进行，配有放松音乐。结束后，你会感觉像睡了两个小时一样神清气爽。（00:54:00）尤其是对于下午容易疲倦的人来说，如果把这个练习安排在下午1点到3点之间，能让你下午精力充沛，不至于累瘫在沙发上。所以我觉得这对提升内感知能力很有帮助，能让身体放松下来，避免一整天都处于高度紧张的交感神经状态。这样能给身体休息的机会，感觉真的很棒。说实话，这是我教授的所有技巧中播放次数最多的，很多人每天都会听。所以我也会把相关信息放在节目笔记里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I imagine if you feel like you've built this emotional debt, this would be a really good exercise to start to do, is that right?
turns.zh: 我想如果你觉得自己背负了情感债务，那这会是一个很好的开始练习，对吧？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah, it is fantastic. I mean, there's some people who struggle with having enough energy to kind of get out of bed and function. But again, I imagine listeners to your show, people that live in Silicon Valley, their challenge is the downshifting without external substances. And so NSDR is a really great way of strengthening that ventral vagal tone, which is our body's capacity to go from on kind of go, go, go to then relaxing. There's a quote from Kevin Kelly that I interviewed recently, and he said, "If you have a great work ethic that needs to be matched with a great rest ethic." And I think that kind of piece of actually training our capacity to downshift after stress is just completely missing from most people's playbooks.
turns.zh: 是的，真的很棒。我知道有些人甚至连起床的精力都没有。但我觉得你们节目的听众，尤其是硅谷的听众，面临的挑战是如何在不借助外部物质的情况下放松下来。NSDR是增强迷走神经张力的绝佳方法，它能帮助身体从紧绷状态过渡到放松状态。我最近采访了凯文·凯利，他说：“如果你有很强的职业道德，就必须配上同样强大的休息伦理。” 我觉得对大多数人来说，学会在压力后放松的能力完全被忽视了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think with a lot of the sort of advice, if you listen, Tim Ferriss and Huberman and everyone's got this stuff you should be doing every day list and it ends up being so long and there's so many things to do, cold plunge, sauna. What is it that you practice or come back to slash what would you recommend people try to do daily that is most impactful of all this stuff we've talked about?
turns.zh: 我觉得很多建议都太复杂了。比如蒂姆·费里斯、休伯曼之类的，每天列一堆应该做的事：冷水浴、桑拿。那么你自己常做的练习，或者最值得推荐的日常习惯是什么？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: First experiment with a bunch of different practices and see which you enjoy and notice how you feel before and then how you feel afterwards. That's kind of the key because once you know that it feels good, you're not going to have to force yourself or motivate yourself to do it. You'll just do it naturally because you know you'll feel great afterwards. I would recommend starting really simple, so starting with the 4, 4, 8 breathing or humming, doing that in the morning for just two minutes, two minutes in the beginning is enough. And I would also recommend listening to the NSDR practice at least once or twice. If you work from home, it's pretty easy after a lunch break, something like that could also be in the evening when you get home as well. Some people use it to help fall asleep. (00:56:52): And then the final thing that I would recommend is if you have the resources and you have access, finding a somatic practitioner or somatic therapist is so [inaudible 00:57:03]. I mean, I emerged a completely different human on the other side of the 200 breathwork journeys. I have a different experience of life basically released so much time. Even my voice sounds different. If you listen to the podcast episodes I recorded four or five years ago, my voice is higher pitched. It just sounds different. It has a different resonant quality to it.
turns.zh: 先尝试各种不同的练习，看看你喜欢哪种，并观察练习前后的感觉差异。这很关键，因为一旦你发现它能带来愉悦感，就无需再强迫自己或激励自己去做这些事了。你会自然而然地坚持下去，因为你知道练习后会感觉很棒。我建议从简单开始，比如进行4次、4次、8次呼吸或哼唱练习，早上只需坚持两分钟即可。刚开始两分钟就足够了。我还建议至少听一到两次NSDR练习。如果在家工作，在午休后进行很方便，晚上回家后也可以练习。有些人用它来帮助入睡。（00:56:52）：最后我要推荐的是，如果你有条件和机会，找一位躯体疗法从业者或治疗师，这真的太棒了[00:57:03]。我在完成200次呼吸练习后，彻底蜕变成一个全新的人。我对生活的体验截然不同，节省了大量时间。甚至我的声音都变了——如果你听我四五年前录制的播客节目，会发现我的声音更高亢了。整体共鸣感也完全不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Okay, awesome. So you've kind of summarized, I was going to try to summarize all the advice you've given, but if you were to do the bare minimum next steps based on this advice, try this 4, 4, 8/3, 3, 6/2, 2, 4. Does 2, 2, 4 work too if you just go real fast I guess?
turns.zh: 哇。好的，太棒了。所以你总结了一下，我本来想把你给出的所有建议都总结一遍，但如果你想根据这些建议采取最基本的下一步行动，可以试试4、4、8/3、3、6/2、2、4。或者如果速度很快的话，2、2、4也可以吧？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, perfect. Okay, so do that for a couple mornings. See how that does try this NSDR practice. We'll link to a recording of how to do that and then was there something else you recommended? Oh, somatic worker, basically maybe a therapist, maybe not someone that helps you with your body.
turns.zh: 好的，完美。好的，接下来几天早上都试试这个NSDR练习。我们会提供如何进行的录音链接。还有你推荐的其他东西吗？哦，躯体疗法师，基本上可能是治疗师，也可能不是专门帮助你调整身体的人。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah, and I'd add in the eight practice for even 15 seconds before the breathing in the morning and after, just so that you notice the difference. And if you do the NSDR, that is basically a 15-minute interoception practice as well. So you're kind of getting two birds with one stone with that practice.
turns.zh: 对，我还建议在早上呼吸练习前后各进行8次练习，哪怕只有15秒，这样你能更明显地感受到差别。如果你做NSDR练习，那基本上也是15分钟的内观练习。这样一来，一举两得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's your perspective on meditation? Does that fit into this? Do you find the NSDR replaces the need for meditation?
turns.zh: 你对冥想有什么看法？它是否适合这个框架？你觉得NSDR能替代冥想的需求吗？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: That is a big topic. I am an avid meditator as what I've done many 10 day silent retreats. I was in a dark room for 10 days.
turns.zh: 这是个大话题。我是个狂热的冥想者，我参加过很多10天的静默修行。在黑暗的房间里待了10天。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: With meditation, I think it really depends on what you are training. It's like saying what's your opinion on exercise? Well, are you training mobility or stamina or strength? It's the same with meditation. You could be training loving kindness. You could be training your focus and attention. You could be training spacious awareness. So I'm a big fan of embodied meditation practices. So this is often the classic vipassana body scan is a good example. Again, I mean that's basically interoceptive practice where you are just moving your attention through different parts of your body over and over and over again for days on end. (00:59:17): In the case of vipassana retreat, meditation is helpful for the specific skill of increasing the psychological space between a stimulus and your response. So if you have some degree of meditation practice instead of getting wrapped up in a certain emotion or we're even believing a certain thought pattern, there's usually an ability to kind of step back a little bit and see if what it's, so there definitely is a place for meditation. But my viewpoint is that we've kind of over-indexed for mindfulness and meditation in over the last 20 years. There's so many apps, there's so there's much talk about it and we've completely forgotten the body-based approaches. So I'm not saying don't meditate. I think meditation for sure has its place, especially if your goal is more of the traditional waking up and seeing through the nature of the self, that's a different kind of path in my opinion. But if you're looking to function more effectively and be more in tune with your body, then there's a whole different category of practices in this bottom up variety that we've touched on today.
turns.zh:
关于冥想，我认为这很大程度上取决于你正在训练的内容。这就好比问你对锻炼的看法一样——你是想训练灵活性、耐力还是力量？冥想也是如此。你可能在训练慈悲心，也可能在训练专注力和注意力。还有空性觉知。因此，我非常推崇具身冥想练习。例如，经典的内观身体扫描就是一个很好的例子。再说一次，这基本上是一种内感知练习，你需要将注意力反复扫描身体的不同部位，持续数日。

（00:59:17）：在内观静修中，冥想对于增加刺激与反应之间的心理空间这一特定技能非常有帮助。假设你有一定程度的冥想修行，而不是被某种情绪所吞噬，或者甚至相信某种思维模式，你通常能够稍微退后一步，审视其本质。因此，冥想确实有其价值。但我的观点是，过去20年间，我们对正念和冥想的重视有些过度了。有太多的应用程序，太多关于它的讨论，我们完全忘记了基于身体的方法。所以我不是说不要冥想。我认为冥想当然有其地位，尤其是如果你目标是更传统的觉醒和看透自我的本质，在我看来这是一条不同的道路。但如果你想更有效地发挥功能，更与身体协调，那么我们今天讨论的这种自下而上的方法就完全不同了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On the topic of bottom up, I imagine you're a big fan of this book that everyone always talks about, The Body Keeps Score, I think it's called. Would you recommend that book? Is it connected in a large part to the stuff you talk about? What do you think of that book specifically? Because I hear about it all with him.
turns.zh: 关于自下而上这个话题，我猜你应该很喜欢那本大家经常谈论的书，叫《身体从不说谎》吧。你会推荐那本书吗？它和你谈论的内容有很大关联吗？你对那本书有什么特别看法？因为我到处都能听到关于它的讨论。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah, it's a good book. It's by Bessal van der Kolk and there's another writer I think Peter Levine says, "The issues are in the tissues." Is basically the concept. And this is the idea that we have these incomplete mobilization reflexes that are stored in our body and often held as tension. It's not strictly true to say that the trauma is in the body. It is actually a cortical map in the brain which kind of tracks these things. But for kind of practical purposes, it looks and feels as if there is stored grief in my right hip or anger in my solar plexus, that's the experience that we have. And the more that you become aware of these sensations and start to develop emotional fluidity essentially, the more that tension is released and the less reactive you become and the more emotional debt you pay off. So I think The Body Keeps The Score, I think a more accurate way would be the body is the scorecard in a way. I think that's kind a slight reframe. And if you're interested in this, the work of Peter Levine, Waking the Tiger is the seminal book on this mobilization reflex stuff that I'm describing.
turns.zh: 是的，那是一本好书。作者是贝丝·范德科尔克，我记得还有个叫彼得·莱文的作者。他说：“问题存在于组织中。”这基本上就是核心概念。我们的身体里存储着许多未完成的动员反射，通常以紧张的形式存在。严格来说，说创伤存在于身体里并不准确。实际上，它是大脑中的皮质地图，追踪着这些记忆。但从实用角度来看，我们感觉右臀存储着悲伤，太阳神经丛存储着愤怒，这就是我们的体验。当你对这些感觉变得更加敏感，并开始培养情绪流动性时，紧张感就会释放，你的反应性也会降低，情绪债务也会减少。所以我认为《身体从不说谎》，更准确地说，身体本身就是记分牌。这是一个微妙的重新构架。如果你对此感兴趣，彼得·莱文的《唤醒老虎》是关于我所描述的这些动员反射的开创性著作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I never need that part of it. And basically it's actually kept in the brain, but it comes across as somewhere in the body.
turns.zh: 我从不需要那部分内容。基本上它实际上存储在大脑中，但在身体某个部位有体现。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fascinating. I want to spend a little time on a new segment that we have in this podcast that I call Contrarian Corner. So let's visit Contrarian Corner, I feel like you'll have something interesting here. So the question is there something that you have a very contrarian opinion about, something that you believe that a lot of other people really don't believe?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。我想花点时间聊聊我们播客中的一个新板块，我称之为"反向思考角"。那么，让我们来探访这个板块吧，我觉得你会发现一些有趣的内容。问题是，有没有什么事情你持有非常反常的观点？或者说，有没有什么事情你认为大多数人都不认同？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: We've already touched on I'm not a big fan of talk based meditation, which will probably get me some comments I would imagine. I'd say the other one that's worth mentioning is I think that we vastly underestimate the impact of burnout, particularly from a bottom line perspective. There was a research report that I did a couple of years ago where we interviewed these leaders and they'd all experienced burnout of some degree. And we said, if you were to estimate how much this costs your startup or business, what would you say? And the median response was a hundred thousand dollars, which I imagine is more than most people would think. (01:02:57): And most people aren't actively investing in burnout insurance. Like it's not something that's on many people's radar besides meditation practices and things like that. And I think part of the reason that the cost is higher is because there are these second and third order consequences of talent attrition, of opportunity costs, lost productivity, you lose great leaders, make shitty decisions in the run up to the burnout itself. There's also this idea of emotional contagion, which there's some research from Wharton I believe, and they show that the leader or the CEO has a disproportionate impact or their emotional state has a disproportionate impact on the people in their team. So something I'd like to say is the nervous system of an organization is a reflection of the nervous system of the CEO. And so I think that's just something which I would like to see talked about more.
turns.zh: 我们之前已经提到过，我不太喜欢基于谈话的冥想，这可能会招来一些评论。我觉得另一个值得一提的是，我们大大低估了职业倦怠的影响，特别是从底线角度来看。几年前我做过一项研究报告，采访了这些领导者，他们都经历过不同程度的职业倦怠。我们问，如果要估算这对你的初创公司或企业的成本，你们会怎么说？中位数回答是10万美元，我想这比大多数人想象的要高得多。（01:02:57）：而且大多数人并没有积极投资职业倦怠保险。除了冥想练习之类的，这件事并不在很多人的关注范围内。我认为成本较高的部分原因在于，人才流失、机会成本、生产力损失等二阶和三阶后果，还有伟大领导者的流失，以及在职业倦怠前期做出糟糕决策。还有情绪传染的概念，据我所知，沃顿商学院有相关研究表明，领导者或CEO的情绪状态会对团队成员产生不成比例的影响。所以我想说的是，组织的神经系统是CEO神经系统的反映。因此，我认为这是一个值得更多探讨的话题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just on this idea of burnout, I don't think you're saying don't work really hard If you want to work really hard, it's that you need to maintain your body and mind and nervous system if you're working insanely hard. If you're working long hours, feel free, but just know there's debt you're building up and you need to be doing things to pay off that debt as you're doing that.
turns.zh: 关于职业倦怠这个话题，我不认为你在说不要努力工作。如果你想努力工作，那就需要维护自己的身体和大脑以及神经系统。如果你长时间工作，随你便，但要知道你正在积累"债务"，在这样做的时候，你需要采取措施来偿还这些"债务"。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Precisely. It is very much like building technical debt in the early days of a startup. It's worth doing, but just do it intentionally. Know that you're doing that and that. So let's say you work really hard for eight months, you give yourself a month or two off to really downshift. And it's also really worth building that nervous system capacity. It's great to be able to push it really hard and focus and then combine it with that rest ethic as well. So do NSDRs, kind of find a way to downshift so that way of working can be sustainable.
turns.zh: 没错。这很像初创公司早期积累技术债务的过程。值得一试，但要故意为之。要清楚自己在做这件事。假设你努力工作八个月，给自己一两个月的休息时间来真正放松一下。培养神经系统能力也非常重要。能够全力以赴、专注，然后再结合这种休息伦理，这样很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Jonny, we reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 乔尼，我们迎来了令人兴奋的闪电问答环节。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，请问你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: I actually had a sense this question was coming and I have the books with me here. The first book is Constellations by David White. This is the book that I've gifted most to friends, I think more than any other book. And he basically has 52 definitions of words like ambition is I think the first word. And his writing, it just blows me away. I open this to a random page, read the definition, and it's probably affected me more than any other book. So that's one that I love. 15 Commitments of Conscious Leadership, which is I imagine has come up before in your podcast. This is by Jim Dethmer and Diana Chapman. They have the Conscious Leadership Group. And this is basically, in my opinion, it's the best leadership book that I've come across and it combines practicality with a lot of great theory. So this is awesome. And then finally, this is a bit out there, but Recapture the Rapture by Jamie Wheal, big fan of Jamie's work, Jamie's writing. This is kind of three books in one. The beginning is addressing the meta-crisis and a lot of the craziness that we're seeing in the world. The second chapter is very related to what we've been talking about, he calls it Hedonic Engineering and it's basically practices for shifting your state of consciousness. And the third is Ethical Cult Building, which I'll leave that there. [inaudible 01:06:22].
turns.zh:
实际上，我预料到这个问题会被问到，而且我这里还带来了相关书籍。第一本是大卫·怀特的《星座》。这本书是我送给朋友最多的一本，恐怕比其他任何书都多。他书中对52个词汇的定义——比如“野心”就是第一个词——其文笔简直令我惊叹不已。我随手翻开一页，读到某个定义时，它对我的影响远超其他书籍。所以这本书深得我心。

接下来是《有意识领导力的15项承诺》，我想这本书在你的播客中也被提及过。这本书由吉姆·德特默和戴安娜·查普曼合著，他们组建了"有意识领导力小组"。在我看来，这是我读过的最棒的领导力著作，它将实用性与深厚的理论基础完美结合，堪称杰作。

最后这本《重新捕捉狂喜》可能有些出乎意料。我是杰米·惠尔作品的忠实粉丝，这本书堪称三本书合而为一。开篇探讨元危机及当今世界的诸多乱象；第二章与我们此前讨论的"享乐工程"息息相关，实质上是通过实践改变意识状态的方法；第三章则是“伦理邪教构建”，这里先按下不表。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: My wife and I love animations and we saw Kubo and the Two Strings recently, which was fantastic. Just so, so great. That and also Wolf Walkers, which was an Apple TV series. Yeah, those have been my two favorite movies I've seen recently.
turns.zh: 我和妻子都喜欢动画片，最近看了《古博与两个弦》，这部片子太棒了。还有《狼行者》，这是Apple TV的剧集。总之，这两部是我近期最喜欢的电影。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you like animated content, check out the Scavengers Reign on HBO. I've mentioned it on this podcast before, but it's incredible. It's a TV show on HBO. So I usually ask, do you have a favorite question you like to ask candidates you're interviewing? But I know you coach people, so to kind of turn this question a little bit around, do you have a favorite question you like to ask executive coaching clients that you work with?
turns.zh: 如果你喜欢动画内容，不妨看看HBO的《Scavengers Reign》。我在播客里提过这部剧，简直令人惊叹。它是HBO的剧集。我通常会问，你有没有最喜欢问面试者的某个问题？不过我知道你给别人做指导，所以稍微转换一下思路，你有没有最喜欢问高管客户的问题？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: I stole this question from a guy Jerry Colonna who's here in Boulder, and the question is amazing. It is so good. It's basically, how are you complicit in creating the conditions that you say you don't want? And so the word complicit there is key because it's not saying in what ways is it your fault, but it's like in what ways were you complicit in creating the conditions for anxiety, for building up emotional debt? And just the question kind of opens up the door to ways in which you are an active participant in creating these challenges in your life. And it's a really rich journal question or a question to explore with a friend, co-founder colleague.
turns.zh: 这个问题是我从博尔德的杰瑞·科洛纳那里借鉴来的，太棒了。它能启发人思考：你如何助长了自己口口声声不想要的现状？这里"共谋"一词很关键，它不是指"错在哪里"，而是指你如何在不知不觉中为焦虑、情感债务的形成推波助澜。这个问题能让人深刻反思自己在制造生活挑战中所扮演的角色。无论是作为日记问题，还是与朋友、合伙人探讨的切入点，都极具价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I remember him sharing that on the Tim Ferriss podcast many years ago and it stuck with me and I often think of it, but I never am complicit of anything that goes wrong. It's never my fault. He has nothing on me. Just kidding.
turns.zh: 我记得多年前在蒂姆·费里斯的播客上听过他分享这个问题，至今印象深刻，但我从不承认自己对任何出错的事有过共谋责任。永远不是我的错。他说我比他强多了。开玩笑的。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Excellent.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: One is these blue blocking glasses. These are raw optics, blue blocker glasses. They block out a hundred percent of blue light and they are a lifesaver if I'm ever going out of the house basically after dark, I'll wear these to drive. I'll wear these to even dinners with friends sometimes. And it basically means that I'm able to then sleep well that evening. So that's one. (01:08:38): And then the other thing I'll briefly share, this came through the other day, you mentioned the vagus nerve earlier and that device, I have three devices here that are all vagus nerve stimulation devices. This one is called Neuro Sim. This one I believe is Pulsetto, and I think this is a Apollo Strap. I haven't used them that much yet, but they basically work by sending low level electrical stimulation directly to your vagus nerve. So this clips on your ear because the vagus nerve goes through the right side of the neck. Same with Pulsetto. And I'm really curious to compare the effect of these versus say breathwork, humming, the other body-based practices. Obviously, you can do both at the same time, but I am just interested in playing. So I wouldn't recommend them yet, but I think it's interesting that they exist.
turns.zh: 其中之一就是这些蓝光阻隔眼镜。这些是原始光学产品，蓝光阻隔眼镜。它们能百分百阻隔蓝光，如果我晚上出门后开车，或者和朋友共进晚餐，这些眼镜就能派上用场。关键是，这样一来我当晚就能睡个好觉。这就是第一个例子。（01:08:38）接下来，我要简要分享一下前几天收到的产品。你之前提到的迷走神经装置，这里有三个迷走神经刺激设备。其中一个叫Neuro Sim，另一个可能是Pulsetto，还有一个是Apollo Strap。我还没怎么用过它们，但它们的工作原理是通过低强度电刺激直接作用于迷走神经。这些设备夹在耳朵上，因为迷走神经穿过颈部右侧。Pulsetto也是如此。我很好奇想比较一下它们的效果和呼吸法、哼唱等身体实践相比如何。显然，两者可以同时进行，但我只是好奇想试试看。所以目前我不推荐使用，但觉得它们的存在挺有趣的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How cool would that be? We just put these things on, we don't have to do anything else. We just get up, slap on our device and life is amazing. Don't have to meditate, don't have to breathe in a different way. I'm going to need to do this while I'm on the podcast just wear all these devices, see how that goes. Awesome. Well, I guess somehow report back to us how these go because that feels really great. Next question, do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to share with friends, either in work or in life?
turns.zh: 那该有多酷啊？我们只需戴上这些设备，不需要做其他任何事。我们醒来后戴上设备，生活就变得美好。无需冥想，也无需用不同的方式呼吸。我得在播客上试试看，把这些设备都戴上，看看效果如何。太棒了。嗯，我想应该跟大家汇报一下使用效果，因为感觉真的很棒。下一个问题，您有没有最喜欢的处世格言，经常和朋友分享，无论是在工作中还是生活中？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: State over story would be one which we've touched on.
turns.zh: "以状态而非故事为重"就是我们提到的其中一个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: State over story.
turns.zh: "以状态而非故事为重"。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: And then I think the other one, which I think about often is I like to say, "Make generous assumptions." And by that I mean in any situation, what is the most generous story that I can tell of this person, of this situation? Not kind of naively fabricating something, but usually there's a spectrum of I can assume that they're a bad person and they did this thing out of spite, or maybe they had a bad day, maybe they have a lot of emotional debt. There's there's many stories that can be told. And I usually try to have a practice of telling the most generous story that I can.
turns.zh: 然后我觉得另一个我经常思考的是，我喜欢说："要做最慷慨的假设。"我的意思是，在任何情况下，对于这个人、这种情况，我能讲述的最慷慨的故事是什么？不是天真地编造，而是通常存在一个范围——我可以假设他们是坏人，出于恶意才这样做，或者也许他们那天心情不好，又或许他们背负着很多情感债务。可以讲述很多故事。而我通常会努力去讲述最慷慨的故事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that a lot. Another way of describing that is just assume good intentions, which I often think about.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这样描述。另一种说法就是假设善意，我也经常这么想。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. You seem extremely calm always, and very centered and stable. What still gets you rilled up and unsettled, and what do you do when that happens?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你看起来总是非常冷静，非常镇定和稳定。还有什么事情能让你感到激动或不安呢？遇到这种情况你会怎么做？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Well, I was nervous before this podcast, so I did some breathing practices and some stretching and some humming before jumping on here. I still at times notice ways in which I'm conflict avoidant. I've been working on it actively for a while, but there's a part of me that can sometimes avoid conflict. And so I've actually noticed how there's a relationship between that and having a healthy relationship to anger. So basically giving myself permission to express frustration, not at someone, but just allow it to be there. And then from that place set better boundaries with my time with what I'm doing, saying no to certain things. I think that's the practice that's most alive for me right now.
turns.zh: 好吧，在做这期播客之前我特别紧张，所以我做了些呼吸练习、拉伸，还有哼唱。现在我还是会时不时注意到自己有回避冲突的倾向。虽然我已经积极努力了一段时间，但内心深处有时还是会想要逃避冲突。所以我发现这和健康处理愤怒情绪之间存在关联。关键在于允许自己表达挫败感，不针对某个人，而是允许这种情绪存在。然后在此基础上，更好地规划自己的时间和做事边界，学会说「不」。我觉得这才是我当下最需要践行的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Jonny, you are awesome. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online and explore the things that you offer? I think you teach a course, whatever else you offer, talk about that and then how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 乔尼，你太棒了。最后两个问题：听众在哪里能找到你并探索你的服务？我记得你有课程开设，还有其他服务，能不能讲讲？然后听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Yeah, well, this has been so much fun. I am very active on Twitter or X. My handle is Jonny Miller. It's J-O-N-N-Y-M-1-L-L-E-R. And yeah, if this was interesting or listeners would like to dive deeper, I teach a course. Our next cohort is running in the spring, the end of March. Applications are now open, and the website is nsmastery.com/lenny. I've created a custom page and there's a $250 juicy discount for listeners if they want to sign up.
turns.zh: 是的，今天真是太开心了。我在Twitter或X上很活跃，账号是Jonny Miller，用户名J-O-N-N-M-1-L-L-E-R。如果你觉得今天的内容有趣，或者想深入探索，我现在正在教授一门课程。下一期课程将于今年春季开设，具体时间是3月底。申请通道现已开放，网址是nsmastery.com/lenny。我专门为听众创建了一个页面，如果有兴趣报名，现在还有250美元的优惠。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I got to sign up for this myself. I didn't know you're going to do that. That's awesome. And NS Mastery stands for Nervous System Mastery.
turns.zh: 我得自己去报名了。我不知道你要做这个，太棒了。NS Mastery代表的是神经系统掌控力。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Anything else? And then the second question of how listeners can be useful to you.
turns.zh: 太棒了。还有其他问题吗？第二个问题是听众如何能为你提供帮助。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Well, firstly, if any of this resonates, I'd love to hear from you on Twitter or email me as well. I can pass over my email and I would just love it if you experiment with this stuff. I love this idea of just being a scientist of life. So if anything that we've talked about resonates or any of the practices you want to try, just go out and try it and see how it feels and then tell me about it. That would be the greatest gift I think.
turns.zh: 首先，如果你觉得今天的内容有共鸣，我很乐意在Twitter上收到你的反馈，或者直接发邮件给我。我可以把邮箱分享给你，如果你想尝试这些方法，随便试试看效果如何，再告诉我。这对我来说就是最好的礼物。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the best way to tell you about it is tweet at you or is there something else?
turns.zh: 那分享的方式是发推还是有其他途径？

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Tweet at me or my email is jonny@curioushumans.com. So feel free to email me as well.
turns.zh: 发推给我，或者邮箱是jonny@curioushumans.com。也欢迎直接发邮件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right, I'm going to use all these things. Jonny, thank you so much for being here. You're awesome. I am excited for the show notes we're going to have to give people actual tools to use to become less anxious and nervous in their work and life. Thank you again for being here.
turns.zh: 好的，我会把这些都用起来。乔尼，非常感谢你今天的到来。你太棒了。我很期待后续的节目笔记，能给听众提供切实可行的工具，帮助他们在工作和生活中减少焦虑和紧张。再次感谢你的到来。

turns.speaker: Jonny Miller
turns.en: Amazing. Thanks so much, Lenny. This was super fun.
turns.zh: 太棒了。非常感谢，莱尼。今天真的很开心。
